name: Tarsorrhaphy

lead: Tarsorrhaphy is an eye-surgery procedure in which the edges of the upper and lower eyelids are partly joined, usually at the outer corner, so the opening between the lids becomes smaller. It can be temporary or permanent.

Its payoff for appearance is mainly restorative: by protecting the cornea and narrowing an eye opening that is too wide or will not close, it can reduce the exposed, staring look that comes with conditions such as facial palsy or thyroid eye disease, while preserving the eye. It is a treatment for medical problems, and the research on it concerns corneal healing and lid closure.

paras: In clinical practice an ophthalmologist or oculoplastic surgeon places sutures, or sometimes tissue glue, at the lid margins under local anaesthesia, often at the lateral corner. Temporary versions are used while a corneal problem heals or while the lids recover, and permanent ones when the underlying condition persists. Alternatives include eyelid weights, botulinum toxin to induce protective ptosis and other lid surgeries.

Reported complications include failure to protect the ocular surface, the stitches giving way, in-turned lashes, pyogenic granuloma, corneal abrasion, bleeding and infection. Failure is more frequent in patients with prior eye surgery, diabetes or connective tissue disease. Because it reduces the eye opening and can change the look of the eyes, surgeons weigh it against other options.

angle.text: The operation shortens and narrows the eyelid opening, which changes how open the eyes appear. It is used mainly when exposure or lid malposition has medical consequences, and the aesthetic result is a covered, less exposed eye.

lead: Tarsorrhaphy is a surgical procedure in which the eyelids are partially sewn together to narrow the eyelid opening, performed at the corner of the eyelid opening and either temporary or permanent.[1] It is used to protect the cornea in corneal exposure, to treat proptosis such as in Graves ophthalmopathy, to manage eyelid paralysis in conditions such as Mobius syndrome, and to promote healing of corneal injuries.[1]

Its link to appearance is that lid position and eye opening shape how the eyes look. In people whose lids cannot close or whose eyes are exposed, narrowing the opening restores a more protected, covered look while preserving vision. The procedure is not described in the medical sources as a cosmetic operation, and the research on it comes from ophthalmology.[1][2]

Studies include a randomised trial of lateral tarsorrhaphy versus patching for postkeratoplasty epithelial defects,[3] trials of botulinum toxin for protective ptosis,[4] and a registered trial comparing modified tarsorrhaphy with gold weight implants in leprosy-related lagophthalmos.[5]
infobox: Corneal protection, proptosis, facial palsy, corneal healing
Eyelid weight, botulinum toxin ptosis, cyanoacrylate glue

paras: In tarsorrhaphy the surgeon joins the margins of the upper and lower eyelids at one or more points, most commonly at the lateral canthus, which shrinks the palpebral fissure.[1] Variants include temporary suture techniques, permanent surgical fusion, partial gluing with cyanoacrylate, and a caretaker-reversible version described in 2024.[1][6]

Related lid procedures include botulinum toxin injection into the upper lid levator to create a protective ptosis, and placement of a gold weight in the upper lid so that gravity helps it close.[1][4]

Indications named in encyclopedic summaries are corneal exposure, proptosis, and eyelid paralysis, and tarsorrhaphy is used to help corneal injuries and lesions heal.[1] Reviews of neurotrophic keratopathy, a condition of reduced corneal sensation, describe it as one of the surgical options for protecting the surface.[7][8]

Trials include a 36-patient comparison of lateral tarsorrhaphy and tight patching for epithelial defects after corneal transplant,[3] and tarsorrhaphy used alongside mitomycin in pterygium surgery.[9]

Reported complications include failure to protect the cornea, wound dehiscence, trichiasis, pyogenic granuloma, corneal abrasion, haemorrhage and infection. Late referral in thyroid disease raises the risk of corneal ulcers and permanent opacity, and failure is more common after previous eye surgery or in people with diabetes or connective tissue disorders.[1]

A randomised trial of 36 patients with postkeratoplasty epithelial defects compared lateral tarsorrhaphy with tight patching.[3] A multicentre trial evaluated botulinum toxin type A as a way to produce protective ptosis.[4] A registered trial, started in 2019 with 19 participants, compared modified tarsorrhaphy and gold weight implants for paralytic lagophthalmos in leprosy.[5] Another registered trial studies a self-adhering magnetic device for corneal exposure.[10]
